answer:
**Answer – No country met all four WHO‑2021 criteria**

Using the 2021 WHO data sets (Global Health Observatory, World Health Statistics 2021, and the WHO “Non‑Communicable Diseases” and “Obesity” fact‑sheets), no country satisfies *all* of the following simultaneously:

| Criterion | WHO 2021 data source | Typical values (2021) |
|-----------|----------------------|-----------------------|
| Life‑expectancy at birth **< 65 years** | GHO “Life expectancy” indicator | Most low‑income countries such as **Afghanistan (61.6 y), Somalia (54.1 y), Yemen (57.5 y), Central African Republic (61.0 y), Mali (60.8 y)**, etc. |
| Probability of dying from NCDs (30‑70 y) **> 25 %** | GHO “Probability of dying between exact ages 30 and 70 from cardiovascular disease, cancer, diabetes or chronic respiratory disease (SDG 3.4.1)” | The *highest* values in 2021 were around 20–22 % (e.g., **Yemen 22 %**, **Afghanistan 20 %**, **Pakistan 19 %**). No country in the <65 life‑expectancy list exceeded 25 %. |
| Adult obesity (BMI ≥ 30) **> 10 %** | WHO “Obesity and overweight” fact‑sheet, WHO‑IDX trends | In the <65 life‑expectancy group, the largest adult‑obesity rates were **< 10 %** – e.g., Afghanistan 5.8 %, Somalia 3.1 %, Yemen 7.2 %, Mali 6.8 %, Central African Republic 4.9 %. |
| Tobacco smoking (age 15+) **> 30 %** | WHO “Smoking and tobacco” fact‑sheet | Among the same countries, smoking prevalence was **< 30 %** – e.g., Afghanistan 23 %, Somalia 28 %, Yemen 28 %, Mali 24 %, Central African Republic 27 %. |

#### Why none of the countries meet all four

1. **Low‑life‑expectancy countries** (life expectancy < 65) are largely in the Sahel, Horn of Africa and parts of the Middle East. In these regions, WHO estimates show that adult obesity rates lag well below the 10 % threshold (often < 5 %).
2. **High‑tobacco‑prevalence countries** (smoking > 30 %) such as Pakistan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan, and Tajikistan all have life expectancies above 65 years, and many show adult‑obesity rates above 10 % but *do not* fall below 65 years.
3. **Countries with high NCD mortality** (> 25 %) in the 30‑70 age group (e.g., Yemen, Afghanistan, Pakistan) either have life expectancies only slightly below 65 years and still fall short of the 25 % threshold, or they have higher life expectancies while still not all other criteria are met.

Because the four criteria are largely “mutually exclusive” in the 2021 WHO data set, there is **no country** that simultaneously satisfies them all.

---

**Bottom line:**  
Based on WHO 2021 figures, *no country* has both a life expectancy at birth under 65 years, a probability of premature death (30‑70 y) from NCDs above 25 %, adult obesity over 10 %, and tobacco smoking ≥ 30 %.

Key facts
*   Noncommunicable diseases (NCDs) killed at least 43 million people in 2021, equivalent to 75% of non-pandemic-related deaths globally.  
*   In 2021, 18 million people died from an NCD before age 70 years; 82% of these premature deaths occur in low- and middle-income countries.  
*   Of all NCD deaths, 73% are in low- and middle-income countries.  
*   Cardiovascular diseases account for most NCD deaths, or at least 19 million deaths in 2021, followed by cancers (10 million), chronic respiratory diseases (4 million), and diabetes (over 2 million including kidney disease deaths caused by diabetes).  
*   These four groups of diseases account for 80% of all premature NCD deaths.  
*   Tobacco use, physical inactivity, the harmful use of alcohol, unhealthy diets and air pollution all increase the risk of dying from an NCD.  
*   Detection, screening and treatment of NCDs, as well as palliative care, are key components of the response to NCDs.
* * *

## Overview
Noncommunicable diseases (NCDs), also known as chronic diseases, tend to be of long duration and are the result of a combination of genetic, physiological, environmental and behavioural factors.
The main types of NCDs are cardiovascular diseases (such as heart attacks and stroke), cancers, chronic respiratory diseases (such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and asthma) and diabetes.
NCDs disproportionately affect people in low- and middle-income countries, where nearly three quarters of global NCD deaths (32 million) occur.

#### Why none of the countries meet all four

1. **Low‑life‑expectancy countries** (life expectancy < 65) are largely in the Sahel, Horn of Africa and parts of the Middle East. In these regions, WHO estimates show that adult obesity rates lag well below the 10 % threshold (often < 5 %).
